o: Lord and my God, I thank You, for You have given me a new day. I open my eyes and my first thought is of You. You have known me since before I was born, You know where I come from and You know each of my steps. Today I want to place myself in Your hands, with my joys and also my weariness, hiding nothing from You. Thank You for my family, for health and for the roof over my head.

Thank You, because You do not stop at my past or my missteps, but welcome me with mercy. You take what seems small and make something great of it. Change my heart, Lord, as You have changed so many who sought You sincerely. Take from me pride, fear and complaint, and fill my home with gratitude and peace. Make me an instrument of Your goodness.

Guide me throughout this day. May my words be kind, may my hands be ready to help and may my life speak of You at work, in the street and at home. Give me the courage to say a word of hope to someone who needs it. Protect my family and those I love, and sustain those who suffer today. I place everything in Your hands with full trust. In Jesus' name, amen.
h: On this day, November 19, 1862, a boy named William Ashley Sunday, whom the world would know as Billy Sunday, was born near Ames, in the state of Iowa. His father died during the Civil War, and the child grew up in poverty. He spent part of his childhood in homes for soldiers' orphans, far from the comfort other children knew.

Billy discovered that he ran very fast, and that talent led him to professional baseball. Between 1883 and 1887, he played with the Chicago White Stockings and became famous for his speed on the bases. Yet fame did not fill his heart. According to what is reported, during the 1886 or 1887 season, while he was in Chicago, he heard a group of believers from the Pacific Garden Mission singing hymns, and those songs reminded him of the teachings of his childhood. Soon afterward, he gave his life to Christ.

In 1891, he made a decision that surprised many: he turned down a baseball contract of $3,500 a year to work at the Young Men's Christian Association of Chicago for $83 a month. Later, he became a well-known preacher in the cities of his country, calling people to return to God in direct and energetic language. He died in Chicago on November 6, 1935, at the age of seventy-two.

His story reminds us that a person's origin does not limit what God can do with them. A poor orphan child became a witness for Christ to multitudes, not by his own strength, but because one day he let God change his course.
m.c: Today, may you walk with the certainty that God continues to write your story. He cares for every detail of your day and will give you the strength you need. Go out with a quiet heart, for his hand goes before you and his grace accompanies you. Have a good and blessed day!
m: When we look at the life of Billy Sunday, we see that his change began with something very simple: a group of believers singing on a street corner. No one knew those hymns would touch a famous ballplayer. God uses what is small and ordinary to reach hearts, and today you too can be that song on someone's street corner.

The psalmist says that those who sow in tears shall reap with shouts of joy. Sometimes we sow with weariness, with doubts, without seeing any fruit. A kind word, a prayer for a coworker or a gesture of patience may seem insignificant, but God cares for them like seeds. The time of harvest belongs to him, and it will come at the right moment.

Jesus taught that the one who is forgiven little loves little, and the one who is forgiven much loves much. Billy Sunday never forgot where the Lord had pulled him from, and that is why his gratitude moved him to serve. Today you can do the same: remember how many times God has lifted you up, forgiven you and given you another chance. A grateful heart does not stay idle; it looks for ways to bless others.

For today, I propose three steps. First, before leaving your house, thank God for one concrete thing in your life. Second, sow a seed: say a word of encouragement to someone who needs it, or pray silently for that person. Third, if there is something in your life you want to change, present it to God sincerely and take just one step today. He does not ask for perfection, but a willing heart.

o: Heavenly Father, as I end this day, I come to You with a grateful heart. Thank You for the air I breathed, for the bread on my table, for the people You placed on my path and for every moment I felt Your kindness, even when I did not realize it. Blessed are You, Lord, for You have never left me alone. Thank You also for every prayer You heard today.

Forgive me if, today, I busied myself so much with many things that I forgot to sit at Your feet. I acknowledge that weariness and haste rob me of peace. Teach me to choose what is best: Your presence, Your word and the calm that You alone can give. I give You my pending tasks, my worries and everything I could not finish. Tomorrow will be another day and You already hold it in Your hands. Teach me to serve without losing joy.

Watch tonight over my family and my loved ones. Console the sick, accompany those who are alone and give rest to those who cannot sleep. May my sleep be peaceful and may I wake renewed, with a desire to serve You. Thank You for Your love that never fails and for Your peace that surpasses all understanding. In Jesus' name, amen.
h: In the village of Bethany lived three siblings who were friends of Jesus: Martha, Mary and Lazarus. The evangelist Luke relates that, while Jesus was on the road with his disciples, a woman named Martha welcomed him into her home. She was a generous hostess, who wanted everything to be in order to honor her guest.

While Martha was occupied with the preparations, her sister Mary did something different: she sat at Jesus' feet and listened to his word. This was no trivial gesture, for sitting at the teacher's feet was the posture of a disciple who wants to learn. Martha, increasingly tired and burdened with serving, came to Jesus and asked whether he did not care that her sister had left her to do all the serving alone, and begged him to tell her to help.

The Lord's answer was full of tenderness. He said to her: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her.” Jesus did not rebuke her for serving, for service is beautiful. What he did was show her that her busyness had taken her away from what matters most. Notice that he called her by name twice, as one speaks with affection to someone one knows very well.

This scene teaches us that God does not want us to live running and overwhelmed, but to learn to stop beside him. Work has its place, but the relationship with the Lord is the foundation of all the rest. At the end of the day, like Martha, we can lay our rushing at his feet and receive the calm that he alone gives.
t.c: As you close this day, place in the Lord's hands everything you could not settle. He watches over you while you sleep and never grows tired. Rest in peace, with the assurance that his mercy covers you like a warm blanket. May you rise full of new strength.
m: It is very easy to resemble Martha. We all have lists of tasks, people to serve and things to settle. There is nothing wrong with working diligently; Jesus did not criticize Martha's service. What he noticed was her troubled heart. When work takes our peace, something needs adjusting, and the solution is not to stop serving, but to sit down again beside the Lord.

The psalm invites us to bless the LORD by night. The night is a gift, for it allows us to close the door on the rush and look upward. You do not need to have finished everything in order to give thanks. It is enough to lift your empty hands and say: “Lord, today I did what I could; now I rest in you.” This simple prayer is worth more than a thousand frettings.

Notice also that Jesus called Martha by name twice. God does not see you as a machine that produces results, but as a beloved child. He knows your weariness, your worries and also your good desires. There is no reproach in his voice, but an invitation: come, sit down, listen and rest. The good portion he offers will not be taken from you by any problem.

Before sleeping, do these three things. Write on a piece of paper what worries you about tomorrow and give it to God in prayer. Then give thanks for three good things that happened today, however small. Finally, read a verse in silence and let its message accompany you until sleep overtakes you. In this way, your night will be a time of rest and not of anxiety.
